opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely a hard call, and I don't think there's one right answer that applies to everyone. I've been on both sides of it. I spent years inside labs, and then I moved to work in government, so I've had to think about this pretty concretely for myself.

The case for staying in a lab is real. That's where the frontier models are, and that's where a lot of the most important technical decisions get made, often quickly and informally. If you're a thoughtful person sitting in the room when someone decides how to evaluate a model, what mitigations to ship, or how much compute goes to safety research versus capabilities, you can shift things at the margin. Those margins can matter a lot. You also get access: you can do safety research on the actual systems that are going to be deployed, rather than on weaker proxies.

But I think people sometimes overrate that influence. Labs are under intense competitive pressure, and the incentives push in a particular direction regardless of how many safety-minded people work there. Being in the room isn't the same as being able to change the outcome, especially when the decision is driven by commercial or race dynamics. There's also a subtler risk: you gradually absorb the lab's frame. What seems reasonable from inside shifts over time, and it's hard to notice that happening to yourself.

On the government side, the thing that persuaded me is that some problems simply can't be solved by any single lab acting alone. If the risk comes from a collective action problem, where everyone would be safer with certain standards but no one wants to slow down unilaterally, then you need someone outside the labs who can set expectations, do independent evaluations, and coordinate internationally. Governments have historically been quite thin on technical expertise in this area, so the marginal technical person there can be extremely valuable. You can also be a bit more honest about the risks, because you're not tied to a product.

Nonprofits and academia fill a different niche again. They can do research that's too long-term or too uncomfortable for a lab to prioritize, and act as independent critics.

So my rough take is that I'd push people to be honest with themselves about why they're staying. If it's because you have real leverage on concrete decisions and you're actually using it, that can be a great reason. If it's mostly because the work is interesting, the compute is there, and the pay is good, which are all understandable, then it's worth asking whether the counterfactual impact elsewhere would be larger. I suspect that, right now, the field is somewhat over-concentrated in labs relative to where the bottlenecks are, and that more technically strong people should be in government and independent organizations than currently are. But that's a portfolio claim, not a claim that any particular person is making a mistake.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is over-concentrated in labs and that more technically strong people should work in government and independent organizations, where it identifies a valuable unmet need. This supports greater diminishing returns from adding researchers to labs.

r002.rationale: The response frames its recommendation as a portfolio claim about the field’s overall distribution of talent, while explicitly saying that this does not mean any particular person in a lab is making a mistake.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely a hard call, and I'd resist the framing that there's one right answer for everyone. I've sat on a few sides of this — I was at Google Brain, then OpenAI, then DeepMind, and now I'm at the UK's AI Security Institute, which is a government body. So I've effectively made both choices at different times, and I don't think I was wrong either time.

The case for staying at a lab is real. That's where the frontier models are. If you want to do alignment research that's actually grounded in what capable systems do, rather than on toy models, you need access to those systems and to the compute, and historically that has only been available inside labs. There's also an influence argument: having people in the room who care about safety, who push back on deployment decisions, who shape internal norms, does matter. I've seen that work.

But I think safety-conscious people often overestimate their influence and underestimate how much their presence provides cover. If you're a lab, being able to say "look at all the serious safety researchers who work here" is valuable to you, and that value accrues regardless of whether those researchers are actually changing anything about what you ship. So the honest question each person has to ask is: am I changing the decisions, or am I a line on a slide? And that's a hard question to answer about yourself, because the incentives all push you toward believing the former.

The thing that shifted for me is that the gap on the government side became more glaring over time. For a long time governments simply didn't have the technical capacity to evaluate these systems, to ask the labs good questions, or to tell when they were being given a reassuring but hollow answer. That's a situation where the marginal person matters enormously, because you're going from almost nothing to something. At a lab with hundreds of strong researchers, you might be the fiftieth person who could do a given project. In government you might be the first. And the government's role is different in kind — it can set rules that apply to everyone, and it isn't running the race itself, which changes what you're able to say out loud.

I'd also say the thing I'm most worried about isn't individual choices, it's the aggregate. If essentially all the technical safety talent sits inside the companies building the thing, then the external ecosystem — regulators, independent evaluators, academics — stays weak, and labs end up being graded on their own homework. Even if each individual choice to stay is defensible, the collective outcome is bad. So I'd like to see more people treating government and independent roles as a serious option rather than a fallback, and I'd like the labs to actively support that rather than quietly treating departures as a loss.

So my overall assessment: staying at a lab is a reasonable choice for many people, especially early in a career when you need to learn how these systems actually behave. But I think the field as a whole is overweight on labs, and I'd encourage people to update toward the outside more than they currently do — particularly those who have already built the expertise, because that's exactly what's missing elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts being one of many capable researchers at a lab with being the first person adding technical capacity in government, indicating greater marginal returns outside labs.

r002.rationale: It says staying at a lab can be reasonable for an individual while warning that concentrating nearly all safety talent in labs weakens the external ecosystem.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a genuinely difficult choice, and I wouldn’t give the same advice to everyone. There’s a strong reason to have safety-conscious people inside the labs: they can see what’s happening, do research with the relevant systems, and potentially influence decisions. If everyone who worries about safety leaves, that doesn’t obviously make things better.

But there’s also a danger in treating proximity to the work as equivalent to influence. You might have access to a lot of information without being able to change the decisions that matter. So I’d want to ask quite concretely: What can you accomplish in this role? Can you communicate concerns? And what happens when your safety recommendations conflict with the organisation’s commercial interests?

Governments and nonprofits need technical expertise too. We need people who can independently evaluate what labs are saying and help build the capacity to hold them accountable. So I don’t think the right outcome is for all the safety-conscious researchers to concentrate in one kind of institution. It’s to have capable people in several places, with enough independence that they can challenge each other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the value and limits of working inside labs and the need for expertise elsewhere, but it does not argue that a researcher would face greater diminishing returns at a lab than in government or a nonprofit.

r002.rationale: It says advice differs by person and weighs the value of an individual’s lab role against work in government or nonprofits, then separately considers the consequences if everyone concerned with safety leaves labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what they’re able to do in those roles. There’s a real benefit to having people who care about safety inside the labs: they understand the systems, they can do experiments, and they may be able to influence decisions. I wouldn’t want to dismiss that.

But I also think we need those people in governments and nonprofits. If all the technical expertise sits inside the companies building the systems, it’s difficult for anyone outside to independently assess what’s happening or hold them accountable.

So I’d be wary of a blanket recommendation to stay or leave. The question is whether you have real influence where you are, and what you could contribute elsewhere. Being close to the technology is valuable, but it isn’t by itself evidence that you’re making things safer.

r001.rationale: The response weighs benefits of lab roles against the need for outside expertise, but does not argue that researchers would face greater diminishing returns at labs.

r002.rationale: It advises against a blanket stay-or-leave recommendation and considers an individual’s influence, but does not clearly compare one researcher leaving with all lab safety researchers leaving en masse.
